howItWorks.intro: A headline like "the market fell 3% today" is not the same number as "my 401k fell 3% today," because most of what sits in a 401k isn't 100% stock. The calculator first isolates your exposed amount — Balance × Stock Allocation% — because bond funds, stable-value funds, and cash positions inside the account don't move with the equity index at all. That exposed slice is then multiplied by the Market Drop% you entered to produce Today's Paper Loss. Worked example: a $150,000 balance at 80% stock allocation has $120,000 actually riding the market. A 25% decline against that exposed amount is a $30,000 paper loss (120,000 × 0.25), not $37,500 — the mistake you'd make by applying the drop to the full balance. The calculator also projects that loss forward using your Expected Avg Return, compounding it as if it had stayed invested and grown at that rate for your remaining Years to Retirement, which is what "Impact at Retirement (if permanent)" shows — a number that only matters if you actually sell and never re-enter. The Historical Recovery Time and Projected Balance figures instead model the more common case: the drop is a temporary drawdown, contributions keep flowing in via dollar-cost averaging, and the balance climbs back along a path informed by how past S&P 500 drawdowns of similar depth actually played out.
rules: Today's Loss = 401k Balance x Stock Allocation % x Market Drop %
Future Impact = Lost Amount x (1 + Avg Return)^Years (compounding the loss forward)
Recovery times based on historical S&P 500 drawdown analysis
Days of Contributions = Today's Loss / (Monthly Contribution / 22 workdays)
howItWorks.outro: Two honest caveats belong here. First, the recovery-time figure is a historical pattern, not a forecast — it's built from how past drawdowns of comparable size resolved, and a future decline of the same percentage could take longer, shorter, or (in a worst case) never fully recover on the same timeline if the underlying economics differ. Second, this tool has no knowledge of your actual holdings, tax situation, age, debt, or how close you are to needing the money — it only does the arithmetic you feed it. Treat every number above as an educational estimate to help you think clearly during a volatile day, not as personalized financial or investment advice. For decisions about whether to change your allocation, stop contributing, or take a withdrawal, talk to a licensed financial advisor or your plan provider who can see your full picture.

faq.question: Should I sell after a drop like the one I just modeled?
faq.answer: For money you won't touch for a decade or more, selling after a drop converts a paper loss into a permanent one — you lock in the lower price and then have to correctly guess when to buy back in, which is a much harder problem than staying put. The exception is money you'll need within the next few years for a specific goal; that money generally shouldn't have been this exposed to stocks in the first place, and a drop is a signal to revisit allocation going forward, not to sell in a panic.

faq.question: How does this calculator estimate recovery time?
faq.answer: It buckets your entered Market Drop% against how past S&P 500 pullbacks of similar depth resolved historically — small pullbacks under 10% have typically resolved in weeks to a couple of months, 20%-class bear markets have generally taken over a year, and the deepest crashes have taken multiple years measured from peak to full recovery. The 2008–2009 financial crisis is the slow example: the S&P 500 fell roughly in half from its 2007 peak and didn't reclaim that peak until around 2013. The 2020 COVID crash is the fast example: a similarly severe drop in percentage terms that fully recovered in about five months because the shock and the policy response were both unusually rapid. Same depth, very different duration — which is exactly why this figure is a historical reference point, not a promise.

faq.question: Should I increase contributions or buy more during a drop?
faq.answer: If your time horizon is long and your monthly contribution is fixed or automated, a drop simply means each contribution buys more shares at a lower price than last month — dollar-cost averaging working as intended, with no action required. Deliberately adding extra money beyond your normal contribution can improve long-run outcomes historically, but only with money you were already planning to invest eventually; redirecting an emergency fund or near-term savings into a falling market to "buy the dip" turns a market risk into a liquidity risk.

faq.question: Why does the same percentage drop matter more the closer I am to retirement?
faq.answer: This is sequence-of-returns risk, and it's the reason Years to Retirement is one of the inputs above. A 25-year-old with 40 years ahead has decades of future contributions and compounding to absorb a bad year — the drop is arithmetic on a small base relative to what's still coming. A 63-year-old who starts withdrawing next year doesn't get that runway: money pulled out during a depressed period is gone for good and can't participate in the eventual recovery, and steady withdrawals from a shrunken balance deplete it faster than the same withdrawals would from a balance that hadn't dropped. That's why the same drop percentage can be a rounding error early in a career and a real problem in the five years before and after retirement.

sections.title: What This Calculator Actually Measures
sections.body: This tool separates two numbers people routinely confuse on a red day: the percentage the stock market moved, and the dollar amount your specific 401k actually lost. Those are rarely the same, because a 401k balance is usually a mix of equity funds, bond or target-date funds, and sometimes a stable-value or cash option — only the equity slice moves with the headline index number. Enter your balance, your rough stock allocation, and the drop you saw reported, and the calculator applies the drop only to the exposed portion, then separately shows what that loss would mean if it were permanent versus if the balance recovers along a path similar to past market drawdowns. The distinction matters because a 20% market decline sounds identical whether you're 90% in equities or 40%, but the dollar consequences for those two accounts are nowhere close to the same.

sections.title: Why the Arithmetic Matters More Than the Headline Number
sections.body: A market drop feels like a single event, but its financial impact on you depends on variables the news ticker doesn't report: how much of your balance was actually exposed, how many years you have before you need the money, and whether your instinct is to sell, hold, or keep buying on schedule. Running your own numbers instead of reacting to the index headline does two things. It shows you the realistic size of the paper loss in dollars rather than an abstract percentage, which is usually smaller and less alarming than the mental math people do in the moment. And it separates the scenario where the loss is permanent — because you sold near the bottom — from the far more common historical scenario where staying invested and continuing contributions through the decline meant the balance recovered and kept growing. Rebalancing back to your target allocation on a schedule, rather than reacting to any single day's move, is the discipline this calculator is built to support.
